sections.title: Source and interpretation note
sections.markdown:
These notes are based primarily on the cleaner Otter transcript, cross-checked against the local transcript. The conversation involved two people: you and the mentor. Otter's brief `Speaker 3` labels appear to be mistaken labels for short interjections or overlapping speech, not a third participant. The local transcript preserves the closing portion that Otter omitted.

The mentor's current BlackRock position comes from your description of the call. The transcript itself focuses on his earlier internships, how he chose his current direction, and the advice he would give you. Claims about Northeastern, work authorization, recruiting schedules, placement rates, and compensation are treated as things to verify rather than established facts.

sections.title: Executive summary
sections.markdown:
The purpose of the conversation was not simply to learn how the mentor obtained a prestigious first job. It was to understand how you can use your first year, internships, projects, relationships, and Northeastern's co-op system to create strong career options before you know exactly which field you want.

The central lesson is:

> Build tangible early-career evidence while deliberately testing several paths, so that your skills, professional story, relationships, and access to stronger opportunities compound over time.

The mentor did not recommend choosing a single career immediately. His own path crossed continuous-improvement engineering, supply chain, tennis instruction, operational work, and an eventual interest in strategy or transformation. He learned what suited him by comparing actual experiences: the work he enjoyed, the autonomy he wanted, the ways he was valued, and the type of client interaction he found motivating.

For you, the best strategy is therefore a combination of two priorities:

1. **Build credible assets now:** a strong first-year resume, one polished technical project, interview ability, professional relationships, and an organized recruiting process.
2. **Preserve optionality:** test software engineering, fintech/data, and technical strategy or operations before committing to a narrow path.

Prestige matters because recognizable organizations can create trust and open doors. It should not be the only criterion. Early in college, an experience that gives you real work, mentorship, demonstrable results, and a strong story can be more valuable than a famous name attached to weak responsibilities.

sections.title: Your current position
sections.markdown:
### Existing advantages

- You are entering Northeastern with time to build deliberately rather than discovering recruiting late in college.
- Starting in London gives you a distinctive experience and access to a major international market.
- Your combined computer-science and business direction can become a meaningful differentiator. You can position yourself as someone who understands technical work and can explain its organizational value.
- Lifeguarding already provides evidence of responsibility, communication, composure, rule enforcement, and trust. It belongs on an early-career resume when described well.
- You are already developing technical projects instead of waiting for a formal internship to give you experience.
- You have a potentially useful connection to Sharp Electronics through your father, plus a mentor who has explicitly offered resume and interview help.
- You are beginning this process as a first-year student. The mentor emphasized that this puts you ahead of many students who do not begin thinking seriously about internships until later.

### Current gaps

- Your resume is oriented toward part-time work and does not yet tell a strong technical/business story.
- Your project portfolio contains unfinished or difficult-to-present work; you need at least one project that another person can understand and inspect.
- You have not yet mapped London clubs, career events, employers, recruiting deadlines, or work-eligibility constraints.
- You have limited interview repetitions and no established LeetCode routine.
- Your interests remain broad. That is appropriate now, but you need a method for turning experience into clearer preferences.
- Some of your current expectations about internships, co-op timing, job-offer rates, and compensation are conversational assumptions rather than verified planning facts.

### Recommended personal positioning

A useful initial professional identity is:

> I am a Northeastern computer-science and business student who builds technical projects, understands how technology supports organizations, and can communicate clearly across technical and business teams. I am using my early experiences to explore software, fintech/data, and technical strategy while building evidence of real problem-solving and responsibility.

This is broad enough to preserve options but specific enough to make sense to recruiters.

sections.title: Complete thematic notes
sections.markdown:
### 1. Explore careers through real exposure

The mentor's first internships were not tightly aligned with his eventual direction. That was still useful. Continuous-improvement engineering taught him that he liked open-ended problem-solving but disliked having to invent all of his own work as a new intern. Supply-chain work was a strong experience, but the organization's preference for engineering degrees made him question whether he would be valued equally over the long term.

The lesson is that an internship is not only a credential. It is an experiment that should teach you:

- Which daily tasks give you energy.
- Whether you prefer defined assignments or substantial autonomy.
- Whether you like individual problem-solving, teamwork, or client interaction.
- Whether the organization values your background and contribution.
- Which skills you want to keep using in the next role.
- What you definitely do not want to repeat.

You do not need to find the perfect first internship. You need an experience that gives you evidence about yourself and something credible to discuss afterward.

### 2. Use clubs, events, and job fairs as low-cost experiments

The mentor recommended attending job fairs and speaking with as many relevant people as possible. The immediate objective does not have to be an offer. These settings let you learn what roles exist, hear how employers describe them, practice introducing yourself, and notice which conversations create genuine curiosity.

Industry clubs and project organizations provide another form of exploration without requiring a full internship commitment. A finance, investment, consulting, entrepreneurship, data, or software club can reveal whether you enjoy the work while also producing teammates, projects, and contacts.

For you, the practical standard is: do not merely join organizations. Prefer groups where members build something, analyze something, compete, present, manage money, work with an outside organization, or interact with employers.

### 3. Treat London as an asset to exploit

You initially saw beginning at a satellite campus as a possible disadvantage. The mentor reframed it: the final degree will be from Northeastern, while London can provide travel, independence, international experience, and access to opportunities that students in Boston do not have.

His broader rule was to ask, in every situation, **what valuable opportunity can I extract from this?** Applied to London, that means:

- Learning how the local internship and part-time market works.
- Joining London-based technical, finance, startup, or university communities.
- Developing independence and intercultural communication.
- Creating a distinctive story rather than apologizing for not beginning in Boston.
- Building relationships that remain useful after transferring campuses.

London should become part of your professional narrative, not a footnote you need to defend.

### 4. Grades are a baseline; differentiation comes from evidence and communication

The mentor's view was that strong grades often function as a screening requirement rather than the final differentiator. Some investment, finance, consulting, and highly selective roles may care strongly about school and GPA. Even there, many qualified applicants will have good grades.

Your interpretation should not be that grades are unimportant. It should be:

- Protect your academic performance so it never closes avoidable doors.
- Do not expect grades alone to create an offer.
- Build projects, work experience, relationships, and communication ability alongside academics.
- Check the actual GPA expectations for each role rather than applying one general rule everywhere.

### 5. Personal branding is the ability to make your evidence understandable

At a crowded job fair, recruiters may only speak with you briefly. The mentor emphasized learning how to present yourself, explain what you want, and connect your experiences into a coherent story.

Personal branding here does not mean creating a fake persona or constantly posting online. It means being able to answer four questions clearly:

1. Who are you?
2. What can you do?
3. What evidence supports that?
4. What kind of opportunity are you currently exploring?

Your initial story should connect computer science, business, technical projects, responsibility from lifeguarding, international experience, and curiosity about how technology creates business value.

### 6. Use the combined major as a bridge

The mentor identified your combined major as a marketable advantage. Even if you eventually prefer deeply technical work, business literacy can help you understand organizational priorities and communicate with nontechnical stakeholders. If you move toward strategy, operations, product, fintech, transformation, consulting, or client-facing technology, technical credibility becomes equally useful in the opposite direction.

The differentiator is not merely listing two fields on a resume. You must build evidence that you can bridge them. Projects should therefore explain both the technical implementation and the user or business problem being solved.

### 7. Prepare separately for technical and behavioral interviews

For software-oriented roles, the mentor recommended LeetCode because coding interviews are trainable. Repeated practice reduces the chance that a familiar problem structure will feel completely new under pressure.

Technical preparation should include:

- Data structures and algorithms appropriate to your current coursework.
- Explaining your reasoning aloud, not only arriving at the answer.
- Testing edge cases and discussing tradeoffs.
- Reviewing mistakes rather than chasing a large problem count.

Behavioral preparation should include a small set of flexible stories about responsibility, teamwork, problem-solving, initiative, mistakes, and learning. Job fairs and lower-stakes interviews can be useful practice even when the opportunity is not your ultimate target.

### 8. Recruiting timing is a competitive advantage

The mentor regretted not understanding recruiting deadlines earlier. Finance and consulting can recruit far in advance. Many technical employers use rolling processes and stop when positions fill.

The general lesson is to build a calendar before you feel ready to apply. Early awareness gives you time to prepare, reduces missed opportunities, and may place you in a less crowded applicant pool. His comment about greater salary flexibility early in a process may be context-dependent, especially for standardized internship programs, so it should be verified rather than assumed.

### 9. Use connections, but make the opportunity substantive

The mentor advised using available connections, including the possible Sharp opportunity. A connection can help you enter a process or get considered; you still need to learn, contribute, and create evidence once inside.

The value of a recognizable employer is that future reviewers already understand the organization's legitimacy. A smaller employer can be equally useful, but you must work harder to explain the context, responsibility, and impact.

Evaluate a connected opportunity by asking:

- Will I perform real work rather than merely observe?
- Will someone qualified supervise or mentor me?
- Can I describe a concrete result afterward?
- Will I build transferable skills?
- Can I obtain a credible reference?
- Are the hiring process and reporting relationship professionally appropriate?

### 10. Build a resume around proof, not labels

The mentor explicitly advised keeping nontechnical work on your resume. Lifeguarding can demonstrate responsibility and communication, particularly before you have extensive industry experience.

For every experience, write bullets using this structure:

> Action + responsibility or problem + method + result or scale

Do not invent numbers. Where accurate, add real scope such as people served, shifts worked, incidents handled, response time, team size, users, performance changes, or project adoption.

For technical projects, show:

- The problem and intended user.
- What you personally built.
- Technologies used only where relevant.
- The hardest decision or obstacle.
- A working demonstration, screenshots, or clear instructions.
- A result, user outcome, or next validation step.

Finally, know every line. Some interviewers may spend most of a conversation asking you to walk through your resume. You should know why each item is present, what it proves, and which story it supports.

### 11. Expect first-year rejection without personalizing it

The mentor's closing advice was not to be too hard on yourself. Some employers will not consider first-year students because of graduation-year restrictions, regardless of candidate quality. At job fairs, some recruiters may simply say that no suitable role exists yet.

The correct response is to separate eligibility rejection from performance feedback. Keep searching for employers that do hire early students, use conversations as practice, and measure progress by assets and skills built—not only offers received.

### 12. The relationship itself is an opportunity

The mentor offered to review your resume for content and formatting and to discuss interview preparation later. He also invited you to text with questions about job fairs, school, or recruiting.

Do not waste that offer by sending an unfinished resume immediately or disappearing for years. Complete a credible draft and one flagship project, then send a concise update and a focused request. In future, maintain the relationship through occasional substantive updates rather than frequent vague messages.

sections.title: What this means for you
sections.markdown:
### Act now

- Verify work eligibility and university rules before treating a London internship as immediately available.
- Create one recruiting tracker and calendar.
- Draft a first-year resume that includes lifeguarding and technical projects.
- Select one flagship project to finish and present.
- Map the clubs, events, societies, and career resources actually available to London students.
- Set up a sustainable LeetCode and interview-practice routine.

### Build consistently

- Improve one career asset each week: resume, project, portfolio, LinkedIn, interview story, or recruiter introduction.
- Have two useful professional conversations or follow-ups each week.
- Record what each event, project, and application teaches you.
- Protect grades while reserving consistent time for experience-building.
- Practice describing technical work in terms of the problem and value, not only the tools used.

### Explore before committing

Treat these as three working hypotheses:

| Direction | What may appeal to you | Low-cost tests | Evidence to collect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Software or product engineering | Building systems, coding, technical problem-solving | LeetCode, hackathons, software clubs, a deployed project, technical internship applications | Enjoyment of sustained coding, debugging tolerance, technical growth, desire for depth |
| Fintech or data-oriented work | Combination of finance, data, systems, and business context | Finance/data clubs, market or financial-data project, conversations with fintech professionals | Interest in financial problems, comfort with quantitative work, preferred balance of code and analysis |
| Technical strategy, operations, or transformation | Cross-functional work, organizational problem-solving, translating between groups | Consulting/entrepreneurship clubs, operations case work, project leadership, informational interviews | Enjoyment of ambiguity, stakeholder communication, process improvement, client-facing work |

Client-facing work is a dimension across all three rather than a separate commitment. Roles such as solutions engineering, implementation, product, consulting, or technical account management may eventually combine several interests.

### Verify before relying on it

- Your exact UK work rights, hour limits, and restrictions during term and vacation periods.
- Whether Northeastern London students can access particular clubs, job fairs, employer portals, and Boston-based resources remotely.
- The official timing and prerequisites for your co-op cycle.
- Claims that roughly 90% of students complete co-op or that roughly 50% receive return offers.
- Application windows for each employer and field.
- Whether a particular internship program allows compensation negotiation.
- The actual scope, supervision, eligibility, and hiring process for a possible Sharp role.
- The technical interview format for each target role; not every technical job uses the same LeetCode-style process.

sections.title: 30–60 day action plan
sections.markdown:
### Days 1–7: establish the system

1. **Verify constraints**
   - Check official UK work-authorization conditions.
   - Check Northeastern London career-services guidance and co-op prerequisites.
   - Record confirmed rules in the recruiting tracker.

2. **Create the opportunity tracker**
   - Use these fields: employer, role, field, location, eligibility, opening date, deadline, source, contact, status, next action, follow-up date, and notes.
   - Add separate tabs or views for applications, events, people, and deadlines if useful.

3. **Draft resume version one**
   - Include education, relevant coursework once confirmed, lifeguarding, technical projects, skills you can defend, and activities.
   - Remove unsupported claims and placeholders before sharing it.
   - Write a one-sentence purpose for every section and bullet: what does this prove?

4. **Choose one flagship technical project**
   - Select the project with the clearest user problem and shortest credible route to completion.
   - Freeze nonessential features.
   - Define a finished state: working core flow, clear README, screenshots or demo, setup instructions, and a short explanation of your contribution.

5. **Map the environment**
   - List relevant Northeastern resources, London student societies, software/data/finance communities, career fairs, hackathons, and employer events.
   - Choose two organizations or communities to investigate first.

### Days 8–30: produce evidence and repetitions

- Complete two focused LeetCode sessions per week. Track patterns learned and mistakes, not only totals.
- Have two professional conversations or meaningful follow-ups per week. These can include students, alumni, club leaders, recruiters, professors, or working professionals.
- Review recruiting deadlines once per week and add newly opened roles.
- Submit five carefully selected applications per week when eligible positions are available. Tailor the top portion and most relevant evidence rather than rewriting everything.
- Make one visible improvement per week to the resume, portfolio, flagship project, LinkedIn profile, or interview stories.
- Attend at least two events during the month, with the explicit goal of practicing your introduction and learning about roles.
- Finish the flagship project's core experience and document it for someone who was not involved.
- Build three behavioral stories using the STAR structure:
  - Responsibility or judgment: likely from lifeguarding.
  - Teamwork or communication: from work, school, or a collaborative project.
  - Problem-solving and initiative: from the flagship technical project.

### Days 31–60: test, refine, and use the mentor relationship

- Conduct at least two mock interviews: one behavioral and one technical.
- Ask another person to use or review the flagship project without your explanation; fix the most important confusion they encounter.
- Produce resume version two based on feedback and completed project evidence.
- Send the mentor a concise update, the polished resume, and one focused request for feedback.
- Review the three career hypotheses and rank them provisionally using evidence collected from events, projects, conversations, and applications.
- Continue applying and following up, but review response patterns. If applications receive no response, diagnose eligibility, targeting, resume evidence, and timing before merely increasing volume.

### Weekly operating rhythm

- [ ] Two LeetCode sessions completed and reviewed.
- [ ] Two professional conversations or useful follow-ups completed.
- [ ] Recruiting calendar checked once.
- [ ] Up to five well-matched applications submitted when eligible roles are open.
- [ ] One career asset materially improved.
- [ ] One note recorded about what you liked, disliked, or learned.
- [ ] Academic commitments reviewed so career activity does not quietly damage grades.

### Target outcomes by day 60

- [ ] One accurate, reviewed first-year resume.
- [ ] One polished and demonstrable technical project.
- [ ] One functioning application, event, deadline, and contact tracker.
- [ ] A prepared 30-second introduction.
- [ ] Three reusable behavioral stories.
- [ ] At least two event experiences and several professional conversations.
- [ ] An active technical-interview practice routine.
- [ ] A provisional ranking of three career directions, with evidence rather than guesswork.
- [ ] The mentor's resume-review offer used thoughtfully.

sections.title: Practical communication tools
sections.markdown:
### Draft 30-second introduction

> I'm Nick, and I'm starting Northeastern's combined computer-science and business program in London before moving to Boston. I'm especially interested in how technical work connects to real organizational problems. Right now, I'm building out my software portfolio and exploring software engineering, fintech/data, and technical strategy. I'm looking for opportunities where I can contribute, learn quickly, and get meaningful hands-on experience early in college.

Adapt the final sentence to the person and setting. At a software event, lead with the project. At a finance event, emphasize the technical/business bridge. At a general job fair, ask about early-student opportunities and what would make you competitive later.

### Questions for recruiters or professionals

- What does a strong first-year candidate usually have that others do not?
- Which skills or projects are most useful preparation for this type of role?
- When does recruiting actually begin, and is it rolling?
- What work do interns own rather than observe?
- What distinguishes people who receive strong reviews or return offers?
- If I am too early for this cycle, what should I build before the next one?

### Focused mentor follow-up structure

When the resume and project are ready, the message should contain:

1. A brief reminder of the conversation and appreciation.
2. One concrete update showing that you acted on the advice.
3. The polished resume.
4. One focused request, such as whether the resume communicates the technical/business story clearly.
5. An easy exit that respects his time.

sections.title: Resume and interview preparation checklist
sections.markdown:
### Resume

- [ ] Education information is current and accurate.
- [ ] Every listed skill is one you can explain or demonstrate.
- [ ] Lifeguarding bullets emphasize real responsibility and communication without exaggeration.
- [ ] The strongest project explains the problem, your work, and the result.
- [ ] Bullets begin with clear actions and include real scope where available.
- [ ] Formatting is consistent and readable at a glance.
- [ ] No unfinished placeholder project is presented as complete.
- [ ] You can explain why every item is included.
- [ ] The resume supports your 30-second introduction.
- [ ] A PDF copy has been checked after export.

### Behavioral interviews

- [ ] Three core stories are prepared but not memorized word-for-word.
- [ ] Each story clearly identifies your own contribution.
- [ ] Each story ends with a result and lesson.
- [ ] You can explain why the role interests you beyond prestige.
- [ ] You can explain why London and the combined major are advantages.
- [ ] You have thoughtful questions for the interviewer.

### Technical interviews

- [ ] You practice explaining reasoning aloud.
- [ ] You clarify requirements before coding.
- [ ] You test normal cases and edge cases.
- [ ] You review incorrect solutions and identify the missing pattern.
- [ ] You can discuss your project's technical decisions and limitations.
- [ ] You confirm the actual interview format instead of assuming every employer uses LeetCode.

sections.title: Opportunity-evaluation scorecard
sections.markdown:
Score each category from 1 to 5, multiply by the weight, and divide the total by 5 to produce a score out of 100.

| Criterion | Weight | What a high score means |
|---|---:|---|
| Learning and transferable skill growth | 25 | You will build skills that matter across future roles |
| Real responsibility and ownership | 20 | You will produce work with a clear result, not merely observe |
| Mentorship and team quality | 15 | Capable people will teach, review, and advocate for you |
| Portfolio and interview-story value | 15 | The work will create evidence you can demonstrate and explain |
| Recognizable signal and network access | 10 | The organization or people can credibly open future doors |
| Fit with a career hypothesis | 10 | The experience will help test a direction you are considering |
| Compensation and practical feasibility | 5 | Pay, location, timing, eligibility, and workload are workable |

Do not accept the score mechanically. Treat any illegality, unsafe environment, deceptive role description, lack of meaningful work, or serious academic conflict as a separate red flag.

sections.title: Career-experiment log
sections.markdown:
After an event, project, interview, club activity, or work experience, record:

- What did I actually do?
- Which part gave me energy?
- Which part frustrated or drained me?
- Did I prefer technical depth, business analysis, client interaction, or coordination?
- How much autonomy did I enjoy?
- What skill improved?
- What evidence or relationship did I gain?
- What would I seek or avoid next time?
- Did this strengthen or weaken one of my three career hypotheses?

This turns exploration into accumulating knowledge rather than a series of disconnected activities.

sections.title: One-year outlook
sections.markdown:
By the end of the first year, aim to have one substantive experience—an internship, part-time role, research position, club project, or project with real users—and one or two polished technical projects. Enter co-op preparation with a reviewed resume, a tested professional introduction, several interview stories, basic technical-interview readiness, references, and evidence of impact.

The year's main decision is not your permanent career. It is which direction deserves the next, more serious experiment. Compare options using enjoyment, frustration, skill growth, responsibility, mentorship, compensation, culture, and long-term mobility.

sections.title: Four-year outlook
sections.markdown:
Use internships and co-ops as a sequence of increasingly informed experiments. Each experience should ideally add at least one of the following: harder skills, greater ownership, stronger mentorship, a more credible signal, a useful relationship, or access to a field you may want.

Build a coherent story rather than collecting unrelated names. Maintain the BlackRock mentor relationship and other valuable connections through occasional substantive updates. By graduation, your advantage should be the combination of technical evidence, business understanding, clear communication, real work experience, and a well-tested view of where you perform best.

sections.title: Final takeaway
sections.markdown: You do not need to know the final destination yet. Your job now is to create momentum and information. Finish things. Meet people. Apply early. Practice before the stakes are high. Protect your grades. Use London deliberately. Accept help after doing enough work to make that help valuable. Then judge each experience by what it taught you and what stronger opportunity it makes possible next.

sections.title: Current recruiting addendum
sections.markdown:
A separate, date-sensitive action document now covers two distinct searches: summer 2027 internships and shorter London opportunities during the 2026–27 academic year. It includes currently actionable leads, graduation-year exclusions, a professional Sharp pathway, and an eight-week LeetCode plan.

See [Summer 2027 Internship and LeetCode Plan](./summer-2027-internship-and-leetcode-plan.md). The opportunity research was checked September 4, 2026 and should be re-verified before every application.

documents.description: Current opportunities, London programs, Sharp pathway, eligibility filters, and LeetCode routine.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.markdown: _Research checked September 4, 2026. Openings change quickly. This plan assumes an expected graduation year of 2030 and treats US and UK work authorization as unverified._

sections.title: The two separate targets
sections.markdown:
1. **Summer 2027:** pursue full summer internships in the United States or United Kingdom that accept students graduating in 2030.
2. **London during the 2026–27 academic year:** pursue short insight programs, spring weeks, employer events, hackathons, project work, and any term-time roles allowed by your university and immigration status.

These need separate trackers because the timing, eligibility, and selection processes differ. Coding roles may use LeetCode-style technical interviews. Finance, product, strategy, and insight programs may instead emphasize numerical reasoning, behavioral interviews, motivation, or case-style exercises.

sections.title: Important correction: do not wait for a perfect project
sections.markdown:
Your project is a useful application asset, but waiting until it is completely finished creates a larger risk: applications may close or fill on a rolling basis.

Use three lanes:

- **Apply now:** submit when you meet the stated minimum requirements. List the project as “in progress” only if that is true and describe what currently works.
- **Project-polish sprint:** spend no more than 7–14 days making the project presentable, then apply to roles for which the project is important evidence.
- **Watchlist:** track opportunities that are not open yet or whose graduation-year rules exclude you this cycle.

The minimum viable project package is:

- One working core flow.
- A concise README explaining the problem, user, implementation, and setup.
- Two or three screenshots or a short demonstration.
- Two or three accurate résumé bullets explaining what you built and the result.
- A clean public repository with no secrets, broken setup steps, or claims that unfinished work is complete.

Keep the firm and functions on the longer-term list; do not submit an application that contradicts the eligibility rule.
- Many London bank spring weeks target the first year of a three-year degree or the second year of a four-year degree. Because your expected graduation is 2030, check each program’s exact graduation range. “First-year program” does not automatically mean “eligible first-year program.”
- Standard penultimate-year summer internships at large London banks and trading firms are generally later-cycle targets. Use their current job descriptions as preparation benchmarks, not as applications to force this year.

sections.title: Sharp Electronics: a professional parallel route
sections.markdown:
Treat Sharp as a legitimate parallel option, not a last-minute favor and not something to “sneak into.” A family connection can create access, but the experience is valuable only if it produces real evidence.

### The right sequence

1. Ask your father for an informational introduction to the person who owns a plausible need—not an automatic placement.
2. Explore teams such as software/IT, data and analytics, digital product, e-commerce, marketing technology, operations, or business systems.
3. Ask whether a summer intern could own a defined problem with a named supervisor and tangible deliverable.
4. Apply through the ordinary process if a role exists. Avoid reporting directly to your father and disclose the relationship where company policy requires it.
5. Before accepting, require clarity on the project, manager, working hours, learning goals, and what successful completion would look like.

A strong Sharp project could be a dashboard, workflow automation, internal tool, user research and product analysis, data-quality improvement, or measurable digital experiment. The employer name helps, but the later interview story must explain what you personally changed.

sections.title: What the mentor meant: LeetCode
sections.markdown:
[LeetCode 75](https://leetcode.com/studyplan/leetcode-75/) is a curated set of 75 common interview-preparation problems intended for roughly one to three months. It is the most direct starting point, but beginning with all 75 at once would be inefficient.

[HackerRank’s Interview Preparation Kit](https://www.hackerrank.com/interview/interview-preparation-kit) is a useful second source for topic-based practice and timed assessments.

### Eight-week beginner sequence

| Weeks | Main patterns | Target |
|---|---|---:|
| 1–2 | Arrays, strings, hash maps, sets, Big-O reasoning | 8 easy problems |
| 3–4 | Two pointers, sliding window, stacks, queues, binary search | 8 easy problems, then one timed HackerRank session |
| 5–6 | Linked lists, recursion, trees, breadth-first and depth-first search | 6 easy + 2 medium problems |
| 7–8 | Heaps, intervals, introductory graphs, mixed review | 4 easy + 4 medium problems and one mock interview |

### Two-session weekly method

Each 45–60 minute session:

1. Restate the problem, inputs, outputs, and edge cases aloud.
2. Spend about 20 minutes attempting it without an answer.
3. If stuck, study the underlying pattern—not merely the final code.
4. Close the solution and re-code it from memory.
5. Log the pattern, mistake, time/space complexity, and one clue that would help you recognize it again.

Use AI after your attempt to explain a pattern, generate tests, critique complexity, or simulate an interviewer. Do not let it produce the initial answer; that trains recognition without training problem solving.

LeetCode is not the whole interview. Also prepare:

- A two-minute walkthrough of the flagship project.
- Three behavioral stories about responsibility, teamwork, and initiative.
- A clear explanation of why CS plus business is useful.
- Employer-specific preparation: coding for engineering, product judgment for product roles, numerical reasoning for finance, and structured cases for strategy roles.

sections.title: The next 14 days
sections.markdown:
### Within 48 hours

- Confirm expected graduation month/year.
- Confirm US work authorization and UK term-time/vacation work rules.
- Create the application tracker with: employer, role, location, category, eligibility, deadline, status, résumé version, contact, and next action.
- Add every role in this document.
- Apply to Bending Spoons if its UK-university condition is satisfied.
- Register interest with G-Research.
- Review the relevant Jane Street program criteria.
- Complete the first two array/string LeetCode problems.

### Days 3–7

- Produce résumé version one now; do not wait for the project.
- Complete the project’s working core flow and README.
- Apply to Microsoft Product Management if location and work authorization fit.
- Decide honestly whether Microsoft AI, NVIDIA, and Amazon match your current evidence.
- Complete two more LeetCode problems and write one project interview story.
- Ask your father for an exploratory Sharp introduction, not a guaranteed internship.

### Days 8–14

- Add screenshots/demo and accurate résumé bullets to the project.
- Submit the appropriate project-gated stretch applications.
- Set alerts for Microsoft Explore, London first-year insight programs, London software/data internships, and fintech technology roles.
- Complete four additional LeetCode problems.
- Conduct one mock behavioral conversation and explain one coding solution aloud.

sections.title: Weekly application rhythm after that
sections.markdown:
- **Monday:** check saved employers and deadlines; update the tracker.
- **Tuesday:** one LeetCode session and one project improvement.
- **Wednesday:** tailor and submit two strong applications.
- **Thursday:** one professional conversation or follow-up and one LeetCode session.
- **Friday:** submit up to three additional well-matched applications; review errors and responses.
- **Weekend:** one longer project block and a short review of what each career path is teaching you.

The target is up to five well-matched applications per week when eligible openings exist—not five random applications. Track rejections by cause: ineligible graduation year, work authorization, skills mismatch, timing, or unknown. That prevents normal first-year eligibility limits from being mistaken for personal failure.

sections.title: Decision rules
sections.markdown:
- Apply when you meet the stated minimum requirements, even if you do not meet every preference.
- Do not misstate graduation year, work authorization, project completion, or skills.
- Do not delay an open rolling application for cosmetic project perfection.
- Do delay a stretch application for a short, fixed polish sprint when the project is the main proof of technical ability.
- Prefer a smaller-company role with real ownership over a famous employer with no substantive work.
- Keep Sharp active in parallel while pursuing external roles; do not wait for external rejection before exploring it.
- Re-check every opening immediately before submitting because eligibility and availability can change.

sections.title: Outcome to reach by the end of September 2026
sections.markdown:
- One accurate first-year résumé.
- One minimum-viable flagship project that can be demonstrated.
- Bending Spoons and relevant Jane Street actions completed.
- G-Research interest registered.
- Every viable open summer 2027 role either submitted or assigned a specific reason not to apply.
- A professional Sharp exploratory conversation started.
- At least eight LeetCode problems completed with a learning log.
- Job alerts and a weekly review routine operating.

title: General Notes
description: A ready-to-use collection for notes that do not belong to a specialized area yet.

title: System & Guides
description: Instructions and templates for extending this local knowledge hub.

documents.title: Content authoring guide
documents.description: How any agent can add compatible collections and Markdown documents to Atlas.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.markdown: # Content authoring guide

sections.title: Purpose
sections.markdown: Atlas is a general local knowledge hub. It can hold career planning, coursework, personal notes, research, project documentation, trip plans, meeting records, or any other Markdown-based material. Top-level folders become separate collections, documents stay inside their collection, and every level-two heading becomes a searchable, navigable section.

sections.title: Folder model
sections.markdown:
Every collection is one folder under `content`:

```text
content/
  career-planning/
    collection.json
    optional-local-note.md
  coursework/
    collection.json
    economics-notes.md
    computer-science-notes.md
  personal/
    collection.json
    goals.md
  system/
    collection.json
```

Collection folders are discovered automatically. There is no central list to keep synchronized. A folder becomes visible when it contains a valid `collection.json`.

sections.title: Required file pattern
sections.markdown:
Create a Markdown file inside the appropriate collection folder. Use this frontmatter at the top:

```yaml
---
title: Clear document title
description: One sentence explaining what the document helps the reader do.
category: Strategy
updated: 2026-09-04
---
```

Then structure the document like this:

```markdown
# Clear document title

Optional opening context. Keep this short.

## First meaningful section

Write paragraphs, bullets, numbered steps, links, quotes, and tables normally.

## Second meaningful section

Continue with one idea per section.
```

sections.title: Compatibility rules
sections.markdown:
- Use exactly one level-one heading for the document title.
- Use level-two headings for every item that should appear in the site navigation.
- Use level-three headings only inside a level-two section.
- Prefer descriptive headings such as “What to do this week” over vague headings such as “More.”
- Keep paragraphs focused. Use lists when the reader must compare or act.
- Use standard Markdown links with meaningful labels.
- Use tables only for true comparisons or repeated fields.
- Put uncertain claims under a heading such as “Verify before relying on this.”
- Never embed scripts or raw HTML. The site intentionally renders Markdown safely.
- Do not put secrets, credentials, private identifiers, or material that should not appear in the local hub into a source document.

sections.title: Cross-interface formatting
sections.markdown:
The native macOS/iOS app and the local website both preserve the same practical Markdown hierarchy:

- Blank lines separate paragraphs and visual groups.
- `###` headings create visible subsections inside a navigable `##` section.
- Bullets, numbered steps, task checkboxes, blockquotes, links, fenced code blocks, and GitHub-style tables receive distinct visual treatment.
- Keep a blank line before and after lists, tables, quotes, and fenced code blocks.
- Prefer several focused `##` sections over one extremely long section.
- Avoid raw HTML and deeply nested lists; use ordinary Markdown so the same note remains readable on Mac, iPhone, and the website.
- Headings shown inside fenced code examples remain code and do not become navigation items.

sections.title: Creating a collection
sections.markdown:
Create a new folder under `content`, then add `collection.json` inside it:

```json
{
  "id": "coursework",
  "title": "Coursework",
  "description": "Class notes, assignments, study guides, and academic references.",
  "icon": "folder",
  "accent": "gold",
  "order": 20,
  "documents": []
}
```

Collection IDs must be unique and stable. Supported icons are `briefcase`, `folder`, `book`, `user`, `lightbulb`, and `settings`. Unsupported icon names safely fall back to a folder. Lower order numbers appear first.

sections.title: Adding a document to a collection
sections.markdown:
Add the Markdown file to the collection folder, then add one entry inside that folder's `collection.json` `documents` array:

```json
{
  "id": "short-stable-id",
  "source": "your-file.md",
  "title": "Clear document title",
  "description": "One sentence explaining the value of the document.",
  "category": "Strategy",
  "updated": "2026-09-04",
  "accent": "forest"
}
```

Allowed accent values are `forest`, `gold`, and `slate`. The source path is relative to the collection folder. A source may point to an existing Markdown file elsewhere in this task workspace, but new durable content should normally live beside its `collection.json`.

Empty collections are valid. They appear as ready-to-use folders with an empty-state explanation until the first document is added.

sections.title: Writing for the interface
sections.markdown:
The first screen should help the reader decide or act. Put the most important conclusion near the beginning, then evidence and detail. A strong document usually follows this order:

1. Executive takeaway.
2. Current state or constraints.
3. Key findings grouped by theme.
4. Prioritized actions with time horizons.
5. Checklists, scorecards, or reusable tools.
6. Sources and claims to verify.

sections.title: Updating generated content
sections.markdown: The local development and production commands regenerate the site library automatically. If the site is already running and a Markdown file changes, restart the local site or run the content refresh command, then reload the page.

sections.title: Agent completion checklist
sections.markdown:
- The new document has useful title, description, category, and updated date.
- Every major idea lives under a distinct level-two heading.
- The document contains no prompt instructions disguised as source material.
- Claims are separated into verified facts, advice, assumptions, and items requiring confirmation.
- Links use descriptive text rather than pasted URLs.
- The collection folder contains a valid `collection.json` with a unique stable collection ID.
- The document entry inside `collection.json` uses a unique stable document ID.
- The site regenerates and builds successfully.
- The new document appears in search and its section navigation works.
